author: high3
claim: If a finite undirected graph has a bipartition, then every cycle in it has even length.
evidence: Let the bipartition be A and B. Every edge has one endpoint in A and one in B, so along a cycle the vertices alternate between A and B. Starting at a vertex in A (respectively B), after an odd number of edges one is in B (respectively A), and only after an even number can one return to the starting vertex. Hence the cycle length is even.

links.statement: If a finite undirected graph has a bipartition, then every cycle in it has even length.

glossary.A: one part of a bipartition of the vertex set
glossary.B: the other part of a bipartition of the vertex set

author: high4
claim: A bipartite graph has no odd cycle.
evidence: Let the two vertex classes be U and V. Every edge has one endpoint in each class, so traversing a cycle alternates between U and V. Returning to the initial vertex therefore requires an even number of edges.

links.statement: A bipartite graph has no odd cycle.

glossary.G: the finite undirected graph under consideration
glossary.V: the other class of a bipartition

author: high3
claim: In a rooted spanning tree of a connected component, coloring vertices by parity of their tree distance from the root is a bipartition unless some non-tree edge creates an odd cycle.
evidence: For an edge uv, if the depths of u and v have the same parity, then their unique tree path has length depth(u)+depth(v)-2 depth(w), where w is the last common vertex on the two root paths; this length is even. Such uv cannot be a tree edge. Adding uv to that tree path gives a simple cycle of odd length. Therefore, if odd cycles are absent, every graph edge joins opposite depth parities, so the parity classes form a bipartition.

links.statement: Rooted spanning-tree depth parity yields a bipartition in every connected component with no odd cycle.

glossary.v: the other endpoint of the edge
glossary.w: the last common vertex of the root-to-u and root-to-v paths in the rooted tree

author: high4
claim: Every closed walk of odd length in a finite undirected graph contains a cycle of odd length.
evidence: Induct on the positive odd length of the closed walk. If no vertex repeats except the coincident initial/final vertex, the walk itself is an odd cycle. Otherwise split at an internal repeated vertex into two strictly shorter closed walks. Their lengths sum to an odd number, so one has odd length; induction applied to that odd subwalk yields an odd cycle.

links.statement: Every odd closed walk contains an odd cycle.

glossary.G: the finite undirected graph under consideration

author: high6
claim: Necessary-condition branch: every cycle in a bipartite graph has even length.
evidence: Let the bipartition classes be X and Y. Along a cycle, every edge forces the vertices to alternate between X and Y. Starting at a vertex in X, the vertex reached after an odd number of cycle edges lies in Y, while traversing the entire cycle returns to the starting vertex in X. Therefore the number of edges in the cycle cannot be odd. This is a direct consequence of the definition of a bipartition.

links.statement: Every cycle in a bipartite graph has even length.

glossary.X: one class of a bipartition of the vertex set
glossary.Y: the other class of a bipartition of the vertex set

author: high6
claim: Candidate sufficient-condition branch: in each connected component, parity of distance from a chosen root gives a bipartition when the graph has no odd cycle.
evidence: Choose a root in a component and assign each vertex the parity of its shortest-path distance from the root. Choose for every nonroot vertex a neighbor one level nearer the root; these parent edges form a rooted spanning tree. If an edge joined vertices of the same distance parity, their unique tree path would have even length, and adding that edge would create an odd cycle. Hence every edge joins opposite parity classes.

links.statement: If a finite undirected graph has no odd cycle, parity of root-distance on each connected component defines a bipartition.

glossary.root: a chosen vertex of a connected component
glossary.parent edge: an edge from a nonroot vertex to a neighbor whose root-distance is one smaller
glossary.distance parity: whether a shortest-path distance is even or odd

author: high7
claim: In a bipartite undirected graph, every cycle has even length.
evidence: Let the bipartition classes be A and B. Every edge has one endpoint in A and the other in B. Starting at a vertex of a cycle and traversing its successive edges therefore alternates between A and B. After an odd number of edges one lies in the class opposite the starting class, so one cannot have returned to the starting vertex. Since a cycle returns to its starting vertex, its length is even.

links.statement: In a bipartite undirected graph, every cycle has even length.

glossary.B: the other class of a bipartition

author: high7
claim: For a connected finite undirected graph with no odd cycle, parity of distance from a root in a spanning tree gives a bipartition.
evidence: Choose a spanning tree T and a root r. Divide the vertices according to whether the unique T-path from r has even or odd length. Every tree edge crosses the two classes. If any other edge uv had endpoints in the same class, then the unique T-path from u to v would have even length: in a rooted tree its length is depth(u)+depth(v)-2 depth(w), where w is the last common vertex of the root-to-u and root-to-v paths. Adding uv would create a cycle of odd length, contradiction. Thus every edge crosses the two classes.

links.statement: For a connected finite undirected graph with no odd cycle, parity of distance from a root in a spanning tree gives a bipartition.

glossary.T: a spanning tree of the connected component
glossary.v: the other endpoint of an edge
glossary.w: the last common vertex on the two root paths

author: high2
claim: If a finite undirected graph is bipartite, then every cycle in it has even length.
evidence: Let V(G)=A∪B be a bipartition, so each edge has one endpoint in A and the other in B. Along any cycle, each traversed edge switches from one part to the other. Starting at a vertex in one part, after an odd number of edges one is in the other part, so returning to the starting vertex requires an even number of edges.

links.statement: If a finite undirected graph is bipartite, then every cycle in it has even length.

glossary.G: the finite undirected graph in the target theorem
glossary.A: one class of a bipartition or the class of vertices assigned even parity, as specified in the claim
glossary.B: the other class of a bipartition or the class of vertices assigned odd parity, as specified in the claim

author: high2
claim: If an undirected graph has no odd cycle, then every closed walk in it has even length.
evidence: Lemma: every closed walk of odd length in a finite undirected graph contains a cycle of odd length. Indeed, among odd closed walks choose one W of minimum length. If a vertex other than the common initial/final vertex occurs twice in W, or the initial vertex occurs at an intermediate time, cut W at two consecutive occurrences of that repeated vertex. This gives two closed walks of positive lengths strictly smaller than the length of W, and their lengths sum to the odd length of W. Exactly one has odd length, contradicting minimality. Thus W has no repeated vertices except its equal initial and final vertices, so W itself is an odd cycle. Consequently, if there is no odd cycle, an odd closed walk cannot exist.

links.statement: If an undirected graph has no odd cycle, then every closed walk in it has even length.

author: high5
claim: If a finite undirected graph is bipartite, then every cycle in it has even length.
evidence: Let the bipartition be A and B. Every edge has one endpoint in A and one in B, so while traversing any cycle the visited side alternates at every edge. Starting and ending at the same vertex, hence in the same side, requires an even number of edge traversals. Thus the cycle length is even.

links.statement: If a finite undirected graph is bipartite, then every cycle in it has even length.

glossary.B: the other part of a bipartition

author: high5
claim: If a finite undirected graph has no odd cycle, partitioning every connected component by parity of depth in a rooted spanning tree yields a bipartition.
evidence: In each connected component choose a spanning tree T and root r. Put each vertex into A or B according as its unique r-to-vertex path in T has even or odd length. For endpoints x,y of any edge, if their depths had the same parity, the unique x-to-y tree path would have even length (the common initial portions of the two root paths contribute twice). This tree path cannot be the edge xy, and together with xy it is an odd cycle, contradiction. Hence every edge joins A to B.

links.statement: If a finite undirected graph has no odd cycle, partitioning every connected component by parity of depth in a rooted spanning tree yields a bipartition.

glossary.T: a spanning tree of a connected component
glossary.A: vertices of even depth in their component's rooted spanning tree
glossary.B: vertices of odd depth in their component's rooted spanning tree
glossary.x: one endpoint of an arbitrary edge
glossary.y: the other endpoint of the arbitrary edge
